analysis.one_liner: Keeps federally subsidized affordable apartments affordable for their full 30-year term.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on May 25, 2023 and received no further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the low-income housing tax credit program, the federal government helps pay for apartments that must stay affordable to low-income tenants for 30 years. But a loophole called the 'qualified contract' option lets owners walk away from that promise after 15 years and convert the building to market-rate rents. This bill would close that loophole for buildings already in the program as of 2023, requiring owners who want out to sell at a price that keeps the rents restricted.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income tenants living in tax-credit apartments that would otherwise convert to market-rate rents after year 15. They keep their affordable rents for the full 30-year commitment. Also, the public gets to keep the affordable units it already paid for, since roughly half of tax-credit buildings have historically exited affordability early through this loophole.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the qualified contract option for any building that received its tax-credit allocation before January 1, 2023, so owners can no longer use it to end affordability early [S2][S3].

If an owner still exits, the bill requires the sale price of the low-income portion of the building to reflect the rent restrictions, meaning the property is valued as affordable housing rather than as market-rate [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners and investors in existing tax-credit buildings, who lose the option to convert to market rate or sell at market value after 15 years. Some developers argue this lowers the expected return on the credits and could reduce future investment in affordable housing.

drawbacks.text: Critics of repealing the qualified contract option argue it reduces the resale value of older tax-credit properties and weakens investor demand for future credits, which could mean fewer new affordable units get built [S2][S3; general knowledge of how tax-credit investment is priced].
The bill is purely protective: it preserves affordability in buildings that already exist but does nothing to create new affordable housing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real and concrete: tenants keep apartments they can afford, and the public keeps the affordable stock it subsidized. The main cost falls on owners and investors, though the claim that repealing the loophole shrinks future housing supply is a serious one that policymakers weigh in other similar proposals. On balance, the bill protects an existing public investment; the tradeoff is the risk of somewhat less private investment in future tax-credit housing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Neguse introduced the bill on May 25, 2023 with one Democratic cosponsor [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and the action history shows no markup, no vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners and investors of tax-credit properties, who keep the ability to exit affordability after 15 years and convert buildings to market rents, along with syndicators who market the credits on those terms.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Owners who can still convert buildings to market rent

for.name: Rep. Joe Neguse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the qualified contract option.

for.name: Rep. (sole cosponsor)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee / Chairman Jason Smith
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or brought the bill up after it was referred; it sat without action until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, so no roll-call split exists; the bill was sponsored by a Democrat with a Democratic cosponsor and died in a Republican-chaired committee that took no action.

industries.industry: Owners and developers of low-income housing tax credit properties
industries.note: The bill removes their option to convert buildings to market-rate rents or sell them at market value after 15 years. That option is what lets them capture the property's full market value at the expense of the affordability promise.

Repeal lowers the expected exit value of older properties, which syndicators say dampens demand for the credits. The same credits also depend on a federal affordability commitment the public pays for.
